title: Reading civilization across scales

blocks.text: A village is not a miniature empire, and a trading network is not a state without a capital. Changes in scale affect more than population and territory. They change the difficulty of moving information, distributing resources and sustaining cooperation. Societies of different sizes face different problems.

A community of familiar people can coordinate through kinship, reputation and shared memory. A city brings strangers into repeated contact and needs records, rules, food supplies and public infrastructure. Larger states and empires must move instructions and resources over long distances. They cannot simply stretch familiar relationships indefinitely.

Expansion creates capabilities and vulnerabilities together. Cities concentrate specialized work and knowledge while becoming more dependent on food from elsewhere. Density facilitates exchange but can amplify disease and the consequences of infrastructure failure. Size alone does not establish progress; institutions and supporting conditions must keep pace.

The timescale matters too. Decades of political decline can coincide with centuries of cultural diffusion. A civilization that persists for a millennium may change its organization rapidly. A comparison must identify both its level and its period, or answers to different questions will be mistaken for a single conclusion.
